rv.q: Lindsay Posner’s excellent, un-tricksy production of the Arthur Miller classic comes with a slatted wooden set and a terrific cast.
But few playwrights can match Miller's ability to combine astute political analysis with poignant humanity and, flaws and all, this richly acted production still hits home.
It's not a perfect piece, and at times it risks ossifying into a creaky relic from the past. But West stops that from happening.
This is a robust, gripping account of a Miller masterpiece – and the perhaps underrated West, 54, can take his place alongside the great past interpreters of the role.
The evening is vivid where it most matters.
It’s a winning performance in a show that hangs together fine but reaches the boil too readily.
After so much noise, the audience certainly are shaken, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re moved.
Posner’s production feels smaller as a result, turning Miller’s great work into something decidedly humdrum.
And this production does it full justice.

This impressive production, with the aid of a stunning cast, in particular Nia Towle and Dominic West, grounds this classic play in a convincing, naturalistic, historical setting that still resonates in a society where politicians love to hunt migrants.
West’s nuanced performance takes Eddie on a journey from a breadwinner and much-loved father figure to an unreasonable, raving tyrant, making his downfall all the more tragic.
He isn't the dangerous and oppressive titan to begin with, but that makes his final scenes more pathetic and heartbreaking.
This faithful revival of Miller’s classic provides a taut tragedy, offering a powerful exploration of the human condition.

cn.t: West delivers a compelling performance in this traditional revival of Miller's tragedy, though critics remain divided on whether Posner's naturalistic approach can escape the shadow of van Hove's acclaimed 2014 production.
